Traditional computational approaches to emotion detection have included both lexicon-based and machine learning-based methods. While lexicon-based approaches offer interpretability and domain inde- pendence, they often struggle to capture contextual nuance in complex narratives. Machine learning methods, though effective within their training domains, require substantial annotated data and face challenges with domain adaptation. Recent ad- vances in natural language processing (NLP), particularly the development of large language models (LLMs), offer new possibilities for automating emotion detection with greater contextual awareness. This study investigates how emotions are repre- sented and perceived in the television series Severance (Apple TV, 2022) through a multi-layered annotation framework based on Parrott’s hierarchical taxonomy of emotions. All nine episodes of season 1 were annotated scene by scene, producing four datasets: human text-only, human multimodal (video + audio + text), and two LLMs. Comparative analyses assessed inter-annotator agreement, modality effects, and temporal and character-based emotion patterns. Results show that multimod- al annotations yield a far richer and more nuanced emotional landscape than text alone, highlighting the decisive role of prosody, gesture, and facial expression in conveying affect. LLMs captured general emotional polarity but failed to reproduce fine-grained distinctions. Character profiles further reveal individualized affective strategies of repression, resistance, and awakening. The findings underscore the inherently multimodal nature of emotional meaning in audiovisual narrative. Moreno-Ortiz, M. García-Gámez Introduction Emotions are a central component of human communication, shaping meaning-mak- ing processes across cultural contexts. Their study has therefore attracted sustained interest from psychology, linguistics, and discourse analysis. Within computational research, this concern has given rise to affective computing (Picard, 1997), a field that seeks to develop systems capable of recognizing and responding to human emotions. Early approaches drew heavily from psychological models of emotion, particularly dimensional models such as the Valence-Arousal-Dominance (VAD) framework (Russell & Mehrabian, 1977), which provided a foundational approach to quantify- ing affective states in affective computing. Within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the task of emotion detection emerged as an extension of sentiment analysis, seeking to identify fine-grained emotions from human language, and thus going beyond the broader polarity distinctions typical of sentiment analysis (Acheampong et al., 2020). Sentiment analysis focuses on the identification and extraction of people’s opinions towards other entities and their attributes (Liu, 2015). Emotion detection poses greater challenges due to the com- plexity of affective meaning (Nandwani & Verma, 2021). Both emotion detection and sentiment analysis, can be approached using lexicon-based or machine-learning based methods, or a combination of both (Moreno-Ortiz et al., 2019). The former represents the simplest approach, which is based on the comparison of the lemma- tized tokens in a text with the corresponding lemmas in the lexicon, and giving them an appropriate score (Puschmann & Powell, 2018). While some implementations also include contextual valence shifters and multi-word expressions (e.g., Moreno- Ortiz, 2017), the majority typically follow bag-of-words approaches (Taboada et al., 2011). Although these lexicon-based methods enabled large-scale annotation and quantitative analysis, their effectiveness was constrained by their reliance on word- level associations and their inability to capture contextual, pragmatic, or multimodal dimensions of emotion. In discourse-rich or narrative settings, where emotions may be implied (or even contradicted by sarcasm), such approaches often fall short (Cam- bria et al., 2017). Machine-learning models, as explained by Öhman (2021b), are sensitive to context and can be combined with large language models (LLMs) for improved performance. Although they typically perform much better than lexicon-based models (De Clercq et al., 2017; Van Atteveldt et al., 2021), they still perform poorly in domains different to those they have been trained on (Aue & Gamon, 2005; Wang & Liu, 2015). The development of machine learning and neural network models offered advances such as the detection of complex textual patterns. Techniques such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs) began to account for compositional aspects of language (Socher et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2016), although these models still required large amounts of annotated data and remained limited in their ability to adapt to new domains (Balahur et al., 2012). A major breakthrough came with the introduction of the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). Instead of using recurrent layers, it relies on the self-attention mechanism, which allows the model to handle all parts of a sequence simultaneously. Building on this foundation, BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) was 1 3 Emotion in Context: Human and AI Perspectives on the Affective… Page 3 of 28 15 introduced by Devlin et al. (2019), which represented the first deeply bidirectional pre-trained language model. BERT-based architectures rapidly became standard baselines for emotion detection due to their capacity to capture nuanced contextual cues that earlier machine-learning models struggled to identify. The Transformer architecture is at the core of the current generation of LLMs, collectively referred to as generative AI, a term that emerged organically and was originally used in reference to Markov chains models. In a very reduced timeframe, LLMs have transformed all aspects NLP, and introduced new possibilities for all NLP tasks, including emotion detection. Models such as GPT (OpenAI, 2025), LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023), and Claude (Anthropic, 2025) offer new avenues of research for automating emotion detection with greater contextual awareness, thus attempting to capture contextual nuance, pragmatic inference, and stylistic variation (Khare et al., 2024). Recent research has investigated whether it is possible to automatically annotate texts containing emotions with ChatGPT: Koptyra et al. (2023) reached the conclusion that although possible, ChatGPT’s annotations do not reach the same degree of quality of human annotations, while Wake et al. (2023) found a reasonable level of reproducibility in ChatGPT’s performance and concluded that the choice of dataset and emotion labels significantly impacts the system’s performance. For their part, Latif et al. (2025) achieved improved results through data augmentation by incorporating samples annotated by ChatGPT. This study compares the performance of two leading generative LLMs (GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5) in detecting emotions using Parrott’s taxonomy (Parrott, 2001). The models were evaluated using a manually annotated gold standard derived from the scripts of Severance (Stiller, 2022), a series recognized for its psychological depth and narrative subtlety. Scenes were manually tagged according to the primary, sec- ondary and tertiary emotions expressed by the characters. By evaluating how these models handled the layered, often ambiguous emotional expression of characters, this research offers insight into the current capabilities of generative LLMs for emo- tion detection and their implications for affective computing and discourse analysis. This study also aims to provide further insights into the relevance that non-verbal language plays in the expression of human emotions, by comparing two sets human annotations: one where annotators had access exclusively to the scripts (i.e., text- only) and one produced while actually watching the series, thus taking into account verbal and non-verbal expression (i.e., prosody, gestures, facial expressions, posture). The first set of annotations was used to measure the performance of the two LLMs that were evaluated in this study; the second set was used to measure the proportion of verbal versus non-verbal emotion expression. Theoretical Background Affective Computing The computational analysis of human emotions has evolved considerably since Picard (1997) coined the term “affective computing” to describe systems capable of recognizing, interpreting, processing, and inferring human affect. What began as 1 3 15 Page 4 of 28 A. Moreno-Ortiz, M. García-Gámez an ambitious vision of emotionally intelligent machines has developed into a mul- tidisciplinary field drawing on psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, and computer science (Poria et al., 2017). Early affective computing research focused on primarily on rule-based systems and basic pattern recognition. However, the advent of machine learning, particularly deep learning architectures, has enabled more sophisticated approaches to emotion detection. The integration of dimensional models such as VAD with computational methods provided early frameworks for quantifying emotions, while advances in natural language processing and computer vision have expanded the field’s capabilities (Zhao et al., 2022). The capabilities of affective computing largely depend on the modalities employed to infer emotions. In multimodal systems, algorithms go beyond the text and ana- lyze facial expressions and vocal tone to detect affective states (Al-Azani & El-Alfy, 2025). Text-based systems, on the other hand, rely on linguistic cues, which entails significant limitations, such as the ambiguity and subjectivity of language (Mantello et al., 2023; Zahiri & Choi, 2018). Emotions are culturally and contextually shaped, and texts often omit crucial non-verbal cues, such as intonation or facial expressions. Moreover, sarcasm and humor often confound emotion detection algorithms, as these forms of expression depend on pragmatics and inference beyond the literal meaning (Kumar et al., 2022). By allowing machines to detect and adapt to human emotional states, affective computing has potential applications across different fields, such as healthcare (Cano et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2023), education (Keerthika et al., 2024), marketing (Pusz- tahelyi, 2020), social media (Chandrasekaran et al., 2021), or security (Butt et al., 2023), among others. Emotion Models Any attempt to manually or automatically classify emotions presupposes the use of an accepted pre-existing schema or taxonomy of emotions. In turn, human emotions present a wide spectrum or continuum of feelings, and arriving at an agreed-upon universal classification is not an easy task, as the selection of emotion categories has itself become a debate. Öhman (2021a) critically examined emotion categorization practices in computational research, and argued that researchers should rethink how emotions are categorized and annotated, as the use of different theoretical frame- works provides distinct emotion inventories with distinct assumptions. Applied projects such as GoEmotions (Demszky et al., 2020), a large-scale dataset for fine- grained emotion classification, demonstrated that the choice of emotion schema had a significant impact on system performance, annotation quality, and the comparability of results across studies. Dimensional Models Dimensional models, particularly the Valence-Arousal-Dominance (VAD) frame- work, have been foundational in affective computing since their introduction (Russell & Mehrabian, 1977). The VAD model represents emotions as points in a three- dimensional space: valence (pleasure-displeasure), arousal (activation-deactivation), 1 3 Emotion in Context: Human and AI Perspectives on the Affective… Page 5 of 28 15 and dominance (control-lack of control). This approach has proven particularly valu- able for computational applications because it provides a continuous representation of emotional states, allowing for the modeling of subtle affective variations and the mapping of discrete emotion categories onto a dimensional space. VAD-based mod- els remain widely used in affective computing for tasks such as emotion recognition from speech, facial expressions, and physiological signs, and many emotion lexi- cons (e.g., ANEW, EmoLex) include VAD ratings for words (Mohammad & Turney, 2013). The dimensional approach has also been integrated with modern transformer- based models, enabling systems to predict both discrete emotion categories and con- tinuous affective dimensions simultaneously. Categorical Models Categorical models define emotions discretely, thus classifying them into distinct categories according to the particular model being used. Ekman’s model, one of the most salient in the literature, distinguishes six basic emotions: happiness, surprise, anger, disgust, sadness, and fear (Ekman, 1992). Plutchik’s wheel of emotions (Plutchik, 2001) proposes eight primary emotions (joy, trust, fear, surprise, sadness, disgust, anger, and anticipation) that serve as the foundation for all others. These emotions are arranged as four pairs of opposites, based on the physiological reaction each emotion creates in animals (joy-sadness, trust-disgust, fear-anger, surprise-anticipation). The wheel is also dimensional, as each primary emotion can vary in intensity and can be blended to express nuanced affective states. Parrott’s classification (2001), in turn, presents a tree-structured list of emotions based on six primary ones: love, joy, surprise, anger, sadness, and fear, as shown on Table 1. Parrott’s model is particularly useful for linguistic and discourse-based research, as it provides a wide array of emotion labels for the annotation of emotional nuance in text. The availability of this large number of labels facilitates annotation work but poses certain difficulties when it comes to calculating agreement. How- ever, its hierarchical design, which maps lower-order emotions to higher-order ones, makes it possible to calculate agreement at different levels. It considers 49 emotions grouped into 10 main ones: reactive, quite posi- tive, positive thoughts, positive and lively, caring, agitation, negative and passive, negative thoughts, negative and not in control, and negative and forceful (Douglas- Cowie et al., 2011). Hybrid Models An approach that bridges categorical and dimensional frameworks is the Hourglass of Emotions (Cambria et al., 2012). This model represents affective states through both discrete emotion labels and four independent but concomitant affective dimen- sions: pleasantness, attention, sensitivity, and aptitude. Each dimension contains six levels of activation. It was specifically designed to address limitations of purely cat- egorical or dimensional approaches in applications such as sentiment analysis and human-computer interaction, and it forms the theoretical foundation for SenticNet, a large-scale semantic resource that combines commonsense knowledge with affective information for concept-level sentiment analysis (Cambria et al., 2018). 1 3 Emotion in Context: Human and AI Perspectives on the Affective… Page 7 of 28 15 Practical Considerations in Model Selection As in any classification task, reducing the number of categories generally simpli- fies the process. Consequently, emotion detection tasks, such as those organized by SemEval (Chatterjee et al., 2019; Kumar et al., 2024), tend to adopt simpler emo- tion models with fewer categories. Although the most widely used frameworks in computational emotion detection are Ekman’s and Plutchik’s, debate persists within the research community regarding which categorical model best captures human emotions (Öhman, 2021a). This has led researchers to frequently adapt existing tax- onomies, combine elements from different frameworks, or develop custom emotion categories tailored to their particular datasets and research objectives: for example, Demszky et al. (2020) used emotions that were detected as salient by Cowen and Keltner (2017) while making sure that their set included Ekman’s emotion catego- ries, but also allowed annotators to suggest emotions that were not among the given options. This study employs Parrott’s schema because of the hierarchical arrangement it proposes, which allows the evaluation of the classification results at the primary level even when the LLM produces secondary or tertiary emotion categories during auto- matic classification. In addition, the model’s extensive vocabulary of emotion labels is well-suited to capturing the emotional expressions characteristic of dramatic dia- logue in narrative contexts, and it provides interpretable labels that facilitate both human annotation and the evaluation of LLM performance in text-based emotion detection tasks. In order to obtain agreement metrics using this this multi-level schema, a custom script was written that re-created the underlying tree structure and was able to calcu- late agreement at any level for any emotion label contained in the schema. Large Language Models Current LLMs are sophisticated statistical pattern recognizers and generators, trained on vast amounts of textual data to predict and generate human-like language patterns (Minaee et al., 2024). As mentioned in the introduction section, their origins extend back to transformer architectures such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), whose pre- training objectives and contextual embeddings form the foundation on which many contemporary LLMs are built. They can perform tasks such as text generation, image description, or question answering, among others (Phogat et al., 2025). Their capac- ity to generate coherent, contextually relevant responses has made them central to modern NLP and conversational systems. As explained by Zhao et al. (2023), the concept of language models has evolved with the advance of artificial intelligence over the decades. While early LLMs mainly aimed to model and generate text data, latest LLMs focus on complex task solving. The rapid progress of such models has had an impact on the growing number of organizations that now produce systems capable of generating coherent and con- textually appropriate outputs from natural-language prompts. Limitations of Current Large Language Models Despite their impressive capabilities, current large language models exhibit several critical limitations that constrain their reliability and trustworthiness in real-world applications. Hallucinations represent one of the most significant challenges, where LLMs generate factually incorrect or entirely fabricated information with apparent confidence. Hallucination is not merely a technical flaw to be engineered away, but rather an inherent limitation of the statistical learning paradigm underlying these models (Xu et al., 2025). Measuring the impact of this issue, however, is extremely complex, as it varies enormously depending on the task and domain. For example, in legal contexts, LLMs have been shown to hallucinate at least 58% of the time when answering case law questions (Dahl et al., 2024). Similarly, medical applications reveal systematic vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks that trigger hallucinations in clinical decision support scenarios (Omar et al., 2025). In other less specialized tasks, modern LLMs display significantly lower rates of hallucinations. A second, well-known issue is that of sycophancy, which refers to LLMs’ ten- dency to prioritize user agreement over accuracy, generating responses that confirm users’ beliefs rather than providing objective information, which creates a tension between alignment with user expectations and factual accuracy, particularly when those expectations include false premises. Studies evaluating GPT-4o, Claude Son- net, and Gemini found overall sycophancy rates of 58.19%, with this behavior partic- ularly pronounced when users present claims with high confidence or cite perceived authorities (Fanous et al., 2025; Rrv et al., 2024). Thirdly, social biases persist systematically across LLMs, reflecting and often amplifying biases present in training data (Gallegos et al., 2024). Recent research demonstrates that even models designed to pass explicit bias tests continue to har- bor implicit biases across race, gender, religion, and other social categories (Bai et al., 2025). These biases manifest in discriminatory decisions, with evaluation studies showing significant differential treatment based on demographic characteristics in critical contexts such as resume evaluation (An et al., 2025). In terms of reasoning, limitations are apparent in moral and logical decision-mak- ing contexts. LLMs have been shown to exhibit amplified cognitive biases compared to humans, including stronger omission bias (preferring inaction over action) and a tendency to flip decisions based on question framing rather than logical consistency (Cheung et al., 2025). These reasoning failures are particularly concerning as they can lead to systematically flawed advice in contexts requiring careful deliberation. Finally, context sensitivity further constrains LLM performance, with evidence that simple changes to system instructions (i.e., the prompt), such as requesting con- 1 3 Emotion in Context: Human and AI Perspectives on the Affective… Page 9 of 28 15 cise responses, can degrade factual reliability by up to 20% (Le Jeune & Berenstein, 2025). This brittleness reflects LLMs’ limited understanding of pragmatic context and their tendency to prioritize stylistic constraints over accuracy. These limitations have substantial implications for the use of LLMs in critical domains and expose the need for careful validation and continued research. In the context of the current study, we attempt to provide an objective measurement of the performance of some of the best LLMs available today in relation to emotion detec- tion in telecinematic discourse. LLMs Used in this Study: ChatGPT and Claude The evaluation of large language model performance relies on a diverse ecosystem of standardized benchmarks designed to assess distinct capabilities across multiple domains. Among the most influential are MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding), which evaluates breadth of knowledge across 57 subjects ranging from STEM fields to humanities (Hendrycks et al., 2021). Reasoning benchmarks include HellaSwag, which tests commonsense reasoning through plausible sentence completions (Zellers et al., 2019), and BBH (Big-Bench Hard), a subset of particu- larly challenging tasks from the larger Big-Bench collection (Suzgun et al., 2023). Conversational abilities are evaluated through MT-Bench, which assesses multi- turn dialogue quality (Zheng et al., 2023), and the Chatbot Arena, a crowdsourced platform where models compete via human preference comparisons (Chiang et al., 2024). To our knowledge no specific benchmark exists for emotion detection. The two LLMs we will be evaluating for emotion detection, GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, are amongst the top-ranked LLMs in these and other benchmarks. ChatGPT1, developed by OpenAI (2025), is perhaps the most widely known chat- bot. The underlying language models have been pre-trained on massive amounts of text data and then fine-tuned to behave as a useful, human-like, assistant. The model encodes prompts as word embeddings, extends context via transformer layers, and generates responses token by token. GPT-5, the latest milestone in OpenAI’s line of generative-pretrained-transformer models, is described by its developers as their smartest and most useful model yet. Unlike earlier models that often excelled only within narrow domains and left it to the user to select a specific model for each task, GPT-5 is intended to perform at a high level across multiple domains and it automati- cally performs optimal sub-model selection. Despite its achievements, GPT-5 is still subjected to limitations, as it can generate plausible but incorrect information (some- times known as “hallucinations”). Claude is a series of LLMs developed by Anthropic (2025). They have been pre- trained to make predictions in large amounts of text, and have been fine-tuned using constitutional AI and reinforcement learning from human feedback (Henshall, 2023). Sonnet 4.5 is the latest iteration in the “Sonnet” line of Claude models and it is designed for autonomy, extended context handling, and integration into complex workflows. Research Design Objectives and Methods This work investigates how emotion is represented and perceived in narrative televi- sion discourse, and how analytical modality (text-based, multimodal, or computa- tional) shapes emotional interpretation. This main goal translates into three specific objectives: 1. To compare text-only versus multimodal human emotion annotation, thus assessing how access to visual and auditory information might alter emotional perception. 2. To evaluate the performance of LLMs in identifying emotions from dialogue scripts, benchmarking them against human annotations. 3. To map the emotional landscape of Severance, analyzing the distribution and evo- lution of emotions across episodes and characters following Parrott’s taxonomy. Corpus Description The corpus consists of the complete first season of Severance (Stiller, 2022), encom- passing nine episodes, 335 scenes, and 49 characters. The dialogue comprises 25,612 words distributed across 3062 individual dialogue entries. The textual component of the corpus was derived from subtitle (SRT) files, which were obtained from Open- Subtitles. We used regular expressions to remove all data except the text itself, char- acter information, and timecodes, resulting in one text file per episode. The files were manually analyzed to identify scenes. Each episode was then converted into a structured JSON file that encoded the episode and scene identifiers, the participating characters in each scene, and an initially empty list of emotions to be filled during annotation. This uniform JSON structure served as the common input for both human annotators and the language models. Timecodes were preserved for future reference, although they were irrelevant in the present study. 1 3 Emotion in Context: Human and AI Perspectives on the Affective… Page 11 of 28 15 Annotation Scheme and Gold Standards Emotion categories followed Parrott’s (2001) hierarchical model, comprising three levels, as shown on Table 1. Each scene could contain one or more emotions per character, depending on the expressive content of the dialogue and, in the multimodal case, accompanying visual or prosodic cues. Annotators were also asked to choose the most specific emotion possible or select a higher-order one if unsure. Two parallel gold standards were developed to capture different perspectives of emotional interpretation: (i) a text-only gold standard (based exclusively on the dialogue scripts), and (ii) a multimodal gold standard (based on the audiovisual episodes). Both were produced through a rigorous three-stage process designed to guarantee reliability and validity: 1. Independent annotation: two trained annotators independently labeled the emo- tions expressed by each character in every scene, using a JSON-aware text editor. 2. Inter-annotator agreement: agreement between annotators was calculated using Cohen’s Kappa (κ) coefficient (1960) for each emotion level and modality. 3. Adjudication: disagreements were resolved through a union strategy, by which any emotion identified by either annotator was retained in the final gold standard. This conservative approach guaranteed maximal recall and preserved the richness of emotional interpretation, especially for subtle or overlapping states. As a result, we obtained two high-quality, scene-level annotated corpora (one text-based and one multimodal) serving as gold standards for model evaluation and comparative analysis. Limitations This study provides valuable insights into emotion detection in audiovisual narra- tive. However, several methodological constraints should be acknowledged, along with directions for future research. The analysis focuses exclusively on Season 1 of Severance, comprising nine episodes of a single television series within the psycho- logical thriller genre. This limited corpus size restricts the generalizability of findings to other narrative genres, formats, or cultural contexts. The series’ distinctive aes- thetic, characterized by emotional restraint, minimal dialogue, and thematic focus on 1 3 15 Page 22 of 28 A. Moreno-Ortiz, M. García-Gámez psychological control, may not represent typical patterns of emotional expression in mainstream television. We focused here on creating an analysis framework that may be used to investigate emotions in audiovisual material, and the limitations of using LLMs for this purpose. Future research will be aimed at testing and extending the proposed framework to multiple series across diverse genres (e.g., comedy, drama, documentary) and cultural contexts to assess whether the observed patterns of multi- modal emotion expression generalize beyond this specific narrative style. In terms of annotation, the gold standards were developed by two trained annota- tors. While this aligns with standard practice in emotion annotation research (e.g., Aman & Szpakowicz, 2007; Bobicev & Sokolova, 2017) and yielded high inter- annotator agreement (κ > 0.80 at primary and secondary levels), involving additional annotators could provide a more robust measure of annotation reliability and cap- ture a wider range of interpretive perspectives. The union strategy employed during adjudication maximized recall but may have introduced some noise by retaining all emotions identified by either annotator, potentially inflating the emotional diversity of the final gold standards. The two language models evaluated in this study (GPT-5 and Claude Sonnet 4.5) operated in text-only mode, receiving dialogue scripts without access to visual or auditory information. Recent multimodal LLMs capable of processing video and audio (e.g., GPT-5 with vision, Gemini) could potentially achieve higher alignment with human multimodal annotations. Additionally, this study evaluated only two LLMs from a rapidly expanding ecosystem; testing additional models (e.g., Grok, LLaMA, Mistral, DeepSeek) would provide a more comprehensive picture of current capabilities in emotion detection. Despite these limitations, the study demonstrates the value of combining human and computational approaches to emotion analysis in audiovisual narrative. The find- ings underscore the fundamentally multimodal nature of emotional expression and highlight current gaps in LLM capabilities for context-dependent affect recognition. Future research addressing these limitations will further refine our understanding of how emotions are encoded, performed, and perceived in narrative media. Conclusions This study set out to examine how emotions are expressed, perceived, and mod- eled in the TV series Severance through a combination of human and computational annotation. Using Parrott’s hierarchical taxonomy of emotions, the analysis drew on four distinct datasets (human text-only, human multimodal, and two text-based LLM outputs) to evaluate the influence of modality, embodiment, and algorithmic interpre- tation on affective understanding. The results show that human multimodal annotations provided the most complete and ecologically valid picture of emotion in the series, revealing how much affective meaning depends on non-verbal cues (e.g., prosody, posture, gesture, facial expres- sion) rather than words alone. The text-only human annotations, while consistent and reliable, captured only the overt linguistic signals of emotion. In contrast, both LLMs displayed limited but measurable sensitivity to emotional tone, performing best at the 1 3 Emotion in Context: Human and AI Perspectives on the Affective… Page 23 of 28 15 primary level of classification. Their relatively low agreement with human annotators underscores the current limitations of text-based AI models in recognizing affect that relies on pragmatic or multimodal context. Comparing text-only and multimodal human data confirmed that emotional inter- pretation is strongly multimodal in nature. When visual and auditory information is available, the range and granularity of recognized emotions expand dramatically, especially at the secondary and tertiary levels. Emotions such as anxiety, frustration, panic, and fondness emerge primarily through performance rather than dialogue, demonstrating that Severance’s affective power resides in its understated physicality (e.g., tone, silence, and gaze) rather than lexical choice. The temporal analysis revealed a pronounced emotional trajectory across the nine episodes. The series evolves from early emotional restraint toward a crescendo of fear, anger, and sadness, alongside brief moments of warmth and solidarity. This gradual escalation mirrors the characters’ awakening to their condition and the disin- tegration of institutional control, resulting in a culmination of affective intensity by the final episodes. At the level of individual characterization, the multimodal annotations expose how each protagonist embodies a distinct emotional strategy. Helly externalizes rebellion through fear and rage; Mark internalizes grief but rediscovers empathy; Milchick weaponizes affect as control; Irving transforms discipline into longing; and Cobel’s repression collapses into fear. Together, they form a small-scale model of emotional control, thus showing how Severance explores the struggle to maintain emotional authenticity in an environment designed to suppress it. Overall, the study demonstrates that emotion in audiovisual narrative cannot be reduced to text. The multimodal dimension is not an embellishment but the primary carrier of affective meaning. Furthermore, the comparison with LLM outputs high- lights how current language models, despite their linguistic fluency, remain limited in their capacity to infer human emotion without embodied or contextual grounding. Future research could extend this work by integrating acoustic and visual data directly into annotation pipelines in order to develop multimodal embeddings capable of cap- turing the full expressive complexity that human annotators can perceive intuitively. In sum, the multimodal analysis of Severance provides a detailed description of how emotions are structured in the series. More generally, it shows that combining computational and human-centered approaches helps to explain how emotions are represented in narrative worlds. The project connects corpus-based annotation with media analysis, thus showing that the study of emotions involves not only what char- acters say or feel, but also how emotion is shown, interpreted, and communicated through multimodal expression. JSON: Name: severance_emotion_pipeline Title: A multimodal hierarchical annotation and evaluation pipeline for fine-grained emotion detection in audiovisual narrative using Parrott taxonomy and large language models Short Hypothesis: Providing multimodal audiovisual context (video + audio + text) to annotators and models causes a statistically significant increase in recall and macro-F1 for secondary and tertiary emotion categories compared to text-only inputs. Related Work: Prior approaches to emotion detection include lexicon-based methods (high interpretability, low contextual sensitivity), supervised machine-learning classifiers (require large annotated corpora and struggle with domain shift), and transformer-based models/LLMs (strong contextual language modeling but limited multimodal grounding and prone to hallucination and sycophancy). Multimodal affective computing systems that fuse audio, visual, and text streams produce improved emotion recognition but often need modality-specific annotations and engineered fusion strategies. Existing hierarchical and hybrid emotion schemas (dimensional, categorical, and hybrid) enable different trade-offs between granularity and reliability; hierarchical taxonomies enable multi-level agreement metrics but increase annotation ambiguity at fine-grained levels. Benchmarks for LLM emotion recognition are scarce, and prior studies show LLMs capture polarity and coarse categories better than fine-grained pragmatic or performance-dependent emotions. Unresolved issues include limited multimodal end-to-end evaluation of LLMs, scarce high-quality multimodal gold standards for narrative media, and the effects of modality ablation on hierarchical label reliability. Abstract: We present a structured research pipeline to quantify how multimodal context affects fine-grained emotion detection in audiovisual narrative and to evaluate current large language models (LLMs) against human performance. The pipeline uses a three-level Parrott taxonomy to produce parallel gold standards: (1) text-only annotations from scripts and (2) multimodal annotations from full audiovisual episodes. The approach standardizes data representation as JSON scene objects, produces adjudicated multimodal and text-based gold standards, and defines evaluation protocols for both supervised classifiers and generative LLMs operating in text-only or multimodal settings. The main contribution is an end-to-end experimental design that measures inter-annotator agreement, modality-driven label shifts, per-category precision/recall/F1, and model confusion at hierarchical levels. Expected outcomes include quantitative estimates of the information gain provided by audiovisual channels for secondary/tertiary emotions, a reproducible benchmark for LLM emotion detection on narrative TV, and empirical characterization of current LLM limitations for multimodal affect inference. Experiments: Datasets: 9-episode Season 1 of Severance segmented into 335 scenes and 3062 dialogue turns; produce two human-annotated gold standards: (A) text-only (scripts/subtitles) and (B) multimodal (video+audio+text). Annotation protocol: two trained annotators independently label each scene-character with Parrott tertiary labels; compute Cohen's kappa per label and level; adjudicate with union strategy to form final gold standards. Baselines: (1) lexicon-based scorer mapped to Parrott primary/secondary labels, (2) supervised transformer (BERT or RoBERTa) fine-tuned on training split, (3) multimodal fusion model (text+audio embeddings+visual frame features) trained end-to-end, (4) GPT-5 zero-/few-shot, (5) Claude Sonnet 4.5 zero-/few-shot, and (optionally) a multimodal LLM if available. Experimental splits for supervised models: stratified scene-level 70% train / 15% dev / 15% test ensuring character distribution parity. Evaluation metrics: per-label precision, recall, F1; macro-F1 at primary/secondary/tertiary levels; Cohen's kappa against gold standard; confusion matrices; coverage (percent scenes with >=1 label). Statistical testing: bootstrap 95% CIs for macro-F1; McNemar for pairwise classifier comparisons; permutation test for modality differences. Ablations and comparisons: (a) human text-only vs multimodal gold standards (measure delta recall/F1), (b) supervised model trained on text-only labels vs trained on multimodal labels, (c) modality ablation for multimodal model (remove audio, remove visual, remove prosody features), (d) hierarchical vs flat label prediction (multi-task: primary + secondary + tertiary vs single-label tertiary), (e) LLM prompt engineering ablation (zero-shot, few-shot, instruction variations). Reporting: per-episode temporal trajectories, per-character emotion profiles, and per-model confusion heatmaps; release evaluation code and JSON-formatted annotations. Risk Factors and Limitations: Single-corpus bias: results derived from one series (genre-specific acting/directing) may not generalize across genres or cultures. Annotation subjectivity: tertiary-level labels have lower inter-annotator agreement, producing noisy gold standards. Class imbalance: rare tertiary categories reduce statistical power and inflate variance. LLM failure modes: hallucination, sycophancy, and prompt sensitivity can distort model outputs and make comparisons brittle. Multimodal alignment errors: inaccurate audio-visual-text synchronization or automatic feature extraction may misrepresent signals. Compute and scalability: multimodal fusion training and evaluation require substantial GPU resources and storage, limiting replication. Legal/licensing: video and subtitle licensing may constrain dataset redistribution. Evaluation metric limits: accuracy and macro-F1 can obscure per-class performance; Cohen's kappa assumes label independence which may not hold in hierarchical labels. Cultural and demographic bias: emotion interpretations may reflect annotators' cultural frames, limiting external validity.
